metaTitle: Consultant forgets to log billable time? Rebuild it on Mac
description: Forgot to log billable time? Rebuild the hours from your Mac calendar, sent mail and files, then enter them honestly. No purchase needed.

intro: If you forgot to log billable time, you can rebuild most of it from the trail you left on your Mac. Start with Calendar, check sent mail and recent files, then enter only the hours you can defend. Do it before the period locks, because a locked week is much harder to fix.
tldr: Start with Calendar on your Mac. Meetings give you the most reliable start and end times.
Use sent mail, Zoom invitations and recent files to fill the gaps around those meetings.
Enter estimates in manual mode with specific descriptions, and label every guess.
Check your firm's lock date first. Locked entries need a manager or admin to change.
Log a little each day from now on, at a fixed time, so the next gap stays small.

blocks.text: What a forgotten timesheet actually costs you

The first cost is the hours themselves. If a week goes unlogged, some of that work may never reach an invoice. A 2016 study by TIQ and London Business School found that about 15% of chargeable consulting work is, in practice, not billed to clients. The study is from 2016, so today's numbers may differ. The direction still matters. Hours that never reach the system never reach the client.

The second cost is the rebuild itself. Piecing a week back together takes longer than logging each day as it happens. Memory also fills gaps with guesses, so the result is less precise than a daily log. I could not find a published study that times reconstruction work. Measure your own next rebuild, then compare it with the short daily habit you would otherwise use.

The third cost is trust. A week of round-number blocks looks like an estimate, because it is one. That is acceptable when you label it. It becomes a problem when a manager sees a sudden jump in hours on a Friday and starts asking questions. At that point the question is no longer about the hours. It is about whether your timesheet can be relied on.

items: Unbilled work: time you spent delivering something that nobody charged for.
Rebuild time: an afternoon of digging through mail and calendars that could have gone to client work.
Challengeable estimates: guessed hours that a client or partner later questions.
Locked gaps: a closed period that leaves hours stuck until someone with admin rights reopens it.
Strained trust: a manager who starts reviewing every line, which slows down both of you.

blocks.text: There is a personal cost too. Kimble's 2017 billing and burnout report found that 35% of workers feel burned out. It is vendor research, and the sample size is not stated, so use the number as a signal. Compare that with the TIQ finding that consultants usually spend 15 minutes a week on timesheets. A weekend lost to rebuilding adds to that feeling.
Why billable hours slip out of the timesheet

Most missed entries come from how logging fits into a working day. The TIQ study measured how often people record their time. About 20% log several times a day, and 18% log once a day. Around 40% log once or twice a week, and 22% log once or twice a month. The less often you log, the more you have to rebuild from memory.

The same study found a quieter problem. About 22% of respondents record less than 70% of their client time, and 38% record between 70 and 90%. Only 40% record 90 to 100%. A gap is common among consultants, so it helps to know the causes before you try to fix one bad week.
How to rebuild missed timesheet hours on Mac

Work from the outside in. Start with the facts that carry timestamps, then fill the gaps with estimates you can explain. On a Mac, Calendar is the best anchor, because most client work starts and ends with a meeting. Go through one missed day at a time, oldest first. Each day you finish makes the next one easier to see.
Start with Calendar on Mac

Apple's Calendar guide lists several ways to add an event on a Mac. You can use Create Quick Event in the toolbar, Siri, dragging in Day or Week view, double-clicking in Day or Week view, double-clicking a day in Month view, or Spotlight in the menu bar. For a missed call, dragging across the time block in Day or Week view is usually the fastest route. Drag the top or bottom edge to fix the start or end time.

items: Open Calendar and switch to Week view for the first missed week.
List each client meeting with its real start and end time. Skip internal meetings unless they were billable.
Add any call that never reached your calendar, so the record matches what happened.
Write the timesheet line for each block while the meeting title is still in front of you.
Check the day's total against your timesheet before you move on to the next day.

blocks.text: Check the trail you already have

Calendar only covers meetings. Other work leaves traces. Look for sent mail on the days you wrote to a client. Check the files you saved or edited, and the Recents list in Finder. If client calls ran on Zoom, the invitations in Calendar or Outlook usually show them too. None of these gives you exact hours. Together they show which days were busy and which were quiet. For sent mail, [Outlook for consultants on Mac](/for/consultants/outlook) covers the basics.

blocks.title: Label every estimate
blocks.text: When a block is a guess, say so in the description. A line such as 'estimated from calendar, prep not logged' is honest and easy to defend. Do not add extra time to make a week look full.
Enter the hours in Toggl Track or your firm's timesheet

If your firm uses Toggl Track, its macOS app has a manual mode for activities that already happened. Toggl's help says manual mode is meant for that. Press ⌘ D, or click the toggle at the top left of the Description field. Then set the start and end times you choose. Toggl's help also says you can switch between timer and manual mode by pressing M.

If your firm uses another timesheet, the buttons will differ, but the rules stay the same. Use one line per client block. Write a description a stranger could follow. Enter only hours you can justify with the trail you checked. Start with the oldest day, and check each day's total against your calendar before you submit.

blocks.title: Do not backdate into a lock
blocks.text: If a period is locked, do not change dates to slip under the lock. A reviewer may read that as falsified records. Ask a manager or admin to reopen the week, and send them the list of days you need.
Locks, confirmed entries, and what a Mac cannot fix

A lock is the real deadline, and it can come sooner than you expect. Clockify's timesheet lock stops regular users from adding or editing entries for a set period. Owners and administrators are not affected, and current or future dates cannot be locked. Clockify describes the lock as a paid feature on its Standard, Pro, and Enterprise plans, so check which plan your firm uses.

Microsoft Shifts works differently. Microsoft's help says you can view and edit timesheets in Shifts on the Teams mobile app, not on desktop or web. That means a Mac cannot make those edits. Confirming a timesheet activity also makes that entry uneditable. The help page does not describe adding a missing clock-in or clock-out, so ask your admin how to correct one.

Some firms lock entries by process rather than software. In that case the lock is a rule, and a rule has an owner. Find out who that is before you ask for a change. A short, specific request gets a clearer answer than an apology with no detail.

blocks.title: Regulated work
blocks.text: If you are a lawyer, nurse, or accountant, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you paste, dictate, or share any entry with an AI tool. Those rules apply to rebuilt timesheets too.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur helps with the reading and the typing around this task. It does not enter your hours, and it does not click for you. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask a question about the screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

items: Point: find the Create Quick Event button or the Description field without hunting through the toolbar.
Guide: walk through a manual entry in Toggl step by step, with you doing each click.
Dictate: hold fn to type a clean description at the cursor, in any app.
Draft: write a short note to your manager asking to reopen a locked week, for you to edit and send.
Everyday: set a reminder in Apple Reminders for your daily log time, by voice.

blocks.text: Lazur does not decide which hours are billable. It does not know your firm's lock dates or client codes unless you say them or they appear on your screen. It looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked and did stays on the Mac.
Mistakes people make when they rebuild hours

items: Filling gaps to reach a full day. A week of perfect totals is the first thing a reviewer questions.
Copying the meeting title as the description. Name the deliverable or decision so the line holds up.
Backdating into a locked period. Ask first, because the lock may be doing a job.
Writing estimates without a label. Unlabelled guesses look like timer readings later.
Waiting for month end. The longer you wait, the more you guess.

blocks.text: Read the week the way a reviewer would. Ask whether each line has a meeting, a message, or a file behind it. Lines with none of those are estimates, and they should say so. Check the total against your calendar, not against a number you want to hit.
Log a little each day so the next gap stays small

The fix for a missed week is a small daily habit. The frequency data shows why. Logging once or twice a week leaves you with a long list to rebuild. Logging at the end of each day leaves you with one short list. Pick a fixed time, close to when you finish client work, and log before you leave your desk.

Make the habit cheap. Keep one line per client in a note, and add the real time as you go. When a call ends, write its description while you still remember it. Dictation helps here. Hold fn and say the description, then check the wording before you save.
Next steps

Start with the oldest missed day, not the whole month. Rebuild that one day from Calendar, check it against the trail, enter it, and check the total. Then ask your manager about any locked or estimated entries. If you want help at the screen, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to point at the control you need, then click it yourself. Current plans are on the [pricing page](/pricing).

faq.question: Can I log hours from last month?
faq.answer: Often yes, but your firm's rules decide it. Toggl's manual mode is built for activities that already happened. Many firms lock periods after a set time, so check with your manager or admin before you enter anything old.

faq.question: What if I really cannot remember a day?
faq.answer: Use the trail first. Calendar, sent mail and recent files can narrow a blank day to a few likely blocks. If the trail runs out, log what you can support, mark the rest as an estimate, or leave it unbilled and tell your manager. Do not invent detail.

faq.question: Is it dishonest to estimate hours?
faq.answer: No, when the estimate is labeled and based on evidence. It becomes a problem when a guess is presented as a timer reading, or when the total is adjusted to hit a target.

faq.question: Does Lazur enter my timesheet for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can point at controls, guide you one click at a time, dictate text at the cursor and draft notes. You still enter and submit the hours yourself.

faq.question: Will Lazur see client names on my screen?
faq.answer: Only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Follow your firm's rules on client data before you use it on a screen that shows client details.

faq.question: What about Microsoft Shifts on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft's help says Shifts timesheets can be viewed and edited in the Teams mobile app, not on desktop or web. Confirmed entries cannot be edited. Ask your admin how a missing clock-in or clock-out should be corrected.

faq.question: How do I stop missing entries from happening again?
faq.answer: Log once a day at a fixed time. The less often you log, the more you have to rebuild from memory. A reminder works better than good intentions at the end of a busy week.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available. For plans and trial details, see the [pricing page](/pricing).

costs.title: Hours that never reach an invoice
costs.text: If a week goes unlogged, some billable work may never be charged. A 2016 TIQ and London Business School study put the figure at about 15% of chargeable consulting work that is, in practice, not billed to clients. The study is old, but the risk is the same today. Hours with no record are hours nobody pays for.

costs.title: Rebuild time you cannot bill back
costs.text: Rebuilding a week is work with no client attached. Hours spent digging through calendars and sent mail cannot be charged. They also come out of time you could have spent on billable work or on rest. Measure your own next rebuild, since I could not find a study that times it.

costs.title: Estimates a client can question
costs.text: A rebuilt timesheet is partly guesswork. When a client or partner asks about a line, you need to explain where it came from. Guessed hours with no trail are hard to defend, and a weak defense can cost more than the hours themselves.

costs.title: Locked weeks that stay open
costs.text: Once a period locks, the fix may need someone else to act. Clockify's lock, for example, stops regular users from editing old entries. That makes a late fix slow, and sometimes impossible without an admin who can reopen the period.

costs.title: Trust, and the energy it drains
costs.text: A manager who sees messy weeks may start checking every line. That adds review time for both of you. Kimble's 2017 report found 35% of workers feel burned out. It is vendor research with no stated sample size, so use it as a signal, not a verdict.

causes.title: No timer during calls and hallway work
causes.text: Calls, quick questions and review sessions rarely start a timer. The work is real, but nothing records it. By Friday those short interruptions have blurred into a stretch you cannot place. Nothing in your day flags them as time to log.

causes.title: Logging happens in batches
causes.text: If you log once a week, you are working from memory of a whole week, not one day. The TIQ and London Business School study found that about 40% of consultants log once or twice a week. Batching feels efficient, but it moves the cost into recall, and recall is where the gaps come from.

causes.title: Switching between clients erases the trail
causes.text: Jumping between projects leaves no clean marker for the hour you just spent. You remember the client but not the task. When you finally log, two clients can blur together, and the hours get split by guess instead of by fact.

causes.title: Codes, rates and task names are hard to recall
causes.text: Firms often use project codes, phases and task categories. Remembering which code applied to a Tuesday review is harder than remembering the review itself. A wrong code is an error a client can spot, so flag the uncertain line rather than guessing a code.

causes.title: Nobody checks until the period closes
causes.text: A timesheet with no reminder sits quietly. Nothing signals that a day is blank until the lock arrives. Without a fixed prompt, the habit depends on willpower at the end of a busy week, which is the worst time to rely on it.

fixes.title: Rebuild from Calendar first
fixes.text: Calendar holds the most reliable timestamps you have. Start there, and add missing calls so the record matches what happened. Do this before you open the timesheet, so you enter from facts rather than from memory of the whole week.

fixes.title: Check the trail before you guess
fixes.text: Sent mail, files and invitations can narrow a blank day to a few likely blocks. Use them to confirm the gaps, and stop when the trail runs out. An honest partial week is better than a complete-looking week you invented.

fixes.title: Mark estimates in the description
fixes.text: Write 'estimated' or 'from calendar' in the description when a number is a guess. That label protects you in a review. It also tells your manager which lines to trust most. It costs seconds per line and saves a long argument later.

fixes.title: Enter in manual mode, oldest day first
fixes.text: Manual mode fits activities that already happened, according to Toggl's help. Work oldest first, so each day's total is clean before the next one starts. Check each day against the calendar, then move on to the next day.

fixes.title: Ask about locks before you backdate
fixes.text: Find the lock date and the person who can make exceptions. If the week is locked, send a short request that names the days and the reason. Admins can reopen a period, and a request with detail gets a clearer answer than a vague one.

fixes.title: Log once a day at a fixed time
fixes.text: Pick one time, and tie it to something you already do, such as closing your inbox. Set a reminder for it. A daily entry needs only a line or two per client, and that turns a painful rebuild into a short check.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Stop the gap from growing
plan.text: Open Calendar and find the oldest missed day. Check the lock date with your manager or admin. Write the open days in a note. Enter nothing yet, so you can see the full gap first.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Rebuild the missed week
plan.text: Work oldest first. Use Calendar, sent mail and recent files to build one line per block. Label every estimate in the description, and stop when the trail runs out.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Enter and check each day
plan.text: Enter the blocks in your timesheet or in Toggl manual mode. Compare each day's total with the calendar. Look into any day that seems too full or too empty before you submit.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Send the exceptions
plan.text: Send your manager a short note about any locked or estimated entries. Name the days, the reason and what you need approved. Send it before the period closes, not after.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set the daily prompt
plan.text: Pick a fixed time to log each day, and set an Apple Reminders alert for it. Lazur can set that reminder by voice if you ask it to.

plan.label: Every day
plan.title: Log before you leave
plan.text: Before you close the laptop, log the day in one line per client. Keep each description short and specific. The habit takes less time than one full rebuild.
